newsitem.title: USA: American, its pilots set for labor talks on Friday.
newsitem.headline: American, its pilots set for labor talks on Friday.

text.p: The first contract talks between American Airlines and its pilots in four weeks is set for Friday, industry sources said Thursday, with a likelihood talks could last into the weekend.

An official at American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp., said the two sides would meet "as long as chairman Harris wanted to meet." The reference was to Robert Harris, head of the Presidential Emergency Board that the White House convened on Feb. 15 to try to resolve the dispute between the nation's second largest carrier and its 9,300 pilots.
An official of the Allied Pilots Association said the union and American would try to reach an agreement before Harris was to submit the board's report to President Clinton, on March 17.
He said the union was ready to meet into the weekend.
Clinton convened the board minutes after the pilots went on strike at midnight on Feb. 14, following a week of marathon, but fruitless, negotiations.
Board members met earlier this month with American and the union to try to find a solution to their contract dispute.
The site of talks is being kept secret so the negotiators can meet away from the glare of the media.
Their earlier talks were held in rooms in a Washington hotel, where reporters crowded the lobby. Both sides held numerous news conferences.
Clinton's decision to convene the emergency board meant the pilots had to return to their jobs for 60 days.
During the first 30 days, the board was to gather information and make proposals for an agreement. The pilots then have another 30 days to decide whether to accept the agreement.

If they reject it, they are free to strike again, although Congress can pass a law to force them to return to work and accept the board's proposed contract or to go into binding arbitration with the airline.
Harris had said he would try to mediate the dispute if there seemed to be a chance for an agreement.

One issue in dispute is wages, with the pilots seeking an 11 percent pay increase to cover the last three years when there were no increases and also the next four years. American offered 6.6 percent.

At issue also is whether the union's pilots, who earn an average of $120,000 a year, will fly the new, small commuter jets American is to buy for its regional airline American Eagle, or whether they will be flown by Eagle pilots, who earn substantially less.
American has said it needed lower-paid pilots in order to be competitive with its rivals who are operating low-cost commuter jet services, but the union wants its pilots in the cockpit.
